newsitem.title: USA: Despite struggles in Midwest, Dole is confident.
newsitem.headline: Despite struggles in Midwest, Dole is confident.

text.p: Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole wrapped up a campaign swing through the Midwest on Friday, saying that although polls showed him behind in the largest of the states he visited, he remained confident.

"Somebody said, 'Why are you in Illinois, you're behind.' I don't think we're behind, I think we're going to win big time," he said at an evening rally on a farm surrounded by vast fields of corn and soybeans.

With his roots in the Midwest, Dole shows a clear affinity for voters in small towns and rural areas. But he trails President Bill Clinton in recent polls in all three states -- Illinois, Ohio and Michigan -- where he campaigned on Friday.
In Illinois, with 22 electoral votes, Clinton had a 54-33 lead in a Mason-Dixon poll last week.

In Ohio, which has 21 electoral votes out of 270 needed for election, Clinton led by 42 percentage points to 36 in an early August Mason-Dixon poll. In Michigan, with 18 electoral votes, Clinton led 47 percent to 29 percent in an EPIC/MRA poll last week.

Dole stuck to his theme of economic revival based on proposed tax cuts and balancing the budget, defending it against criticisms that the twin goals were impossible to reach and saying a more aggressive trade policy would be a complement to his plan.

"When you add it all up, we think it's going to create the growth that we need in America," Dole told a voter forum at Hill Manufacturing, a plant in Wauseon, Ohio near Toledo in the northwestern corner of the state.
"We've got to be more aggressive in our trade policies and that will probably be a subject of some debates when we have debates between myself and President Clinton,"
"We've seen the trade deficit grow and grow and grow in the Clinton administration," Dole said.

Dole also renewed his call for a bipartisan commission to reform Medicare and charged that Clinton campaign ads deceived senior citizens into believing the Republicans would gut the old-age health programme. "Take it (Medicare) out of politics. Stop scaring senior citizens," he said.

Later, Dole joined his running mate, Jack Kemp, at a noisy rally in an airport hangar in Saginaw, Michigan. As he turned up the rhetorical heat in introducing Dole to the crowd, Kemp set a high benchmark for success in the economic programme.

"This economy stinks until one family and one breadwinner can do that which two breadwinners are having to do today," Kemp said. "Bob Dole and Jack Kemp will not stop until there's a job for every American, rising wages for every worker and it will take one breadwinner to do what two breadwinners are doing under Bill's Clinton's economy."

Dole, seeking to answer critics' charges he could not balance the budget at the same time as cutting taxes, told the rally: "We just have to slow the rate of increase in federal spending." He said $393 billion of $576 billion in needed spending cuts had already been passed by Congress this year.

Social Security, Medicare and interest on the federal debt were "off the table," as were more cuts in defence spending. That left spending cuts of about five percent needed from current remaining spending levels of about $600 billion, plus asset sales and additional economic growth to fill the gap.
Dole began the day in Montpelier, Ohio, where he met some distant relatives for breakfast at a Main Street restaurant. He had paid a visit to an ancestral home and gravesite the night before.
Dole tried to cheer up a questioner at the forum in Wauseon who said that despite low unemployment in the area many people in two-income families were unhappy at their jobs and unlikely to vote.
"We've got these miserable folks and they're miserable at their jobs and they're not voting, what can you tell them?" asked the woman, an employee at a local weekly newspaper.
"Well," said Dole, "don't be miserable, but you're going to be happy if Bob Dole is elected."
